🚀 Q-Cast: Real-Time Demand Forecasting System for Quick-Commerce¶

MSc Data Science | Group Project | 2025–26¶

"Predicting what 10-minute delivery customers want — before they order it."

Project Overview:
Q-Cast is an end-to-end machine learning pipeline that forecasts product demand using the M5 Forecasting dataset, simulating a real-time quick-commerce (Zepto / Blinkit / Swiggy Instamart) environment.
The pipeline covers data loading, EDA, preprocessing, advanced feature engineering, three ML/DL models (LightGBM, LSTM, TFT), ensemble forecasting, anomaly detection, and full evaluation.

Dataset Required: M5 Forecasting Competition on Kaggle
Download and place in /data/ folder:

  • sales_train_evaluation.csv
  • calendar.csv
  • sell_prices.csv

📦 Section 1: Setup — Libraries, Seeds & Configuration¶

Install all required libraries, configure random seeds for reproducibility, and suppress noisy warnings.

# ── Set random seeds for full reproducibility ─────────────────────────────────
def set_seeds(seed=SEED):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    os.environ["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = str(seed)

set_seeds()

# ── Helper utilities ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def reduce_mem_usage(df, verbose=True):
    """Downcast numeric dtypes — skips datetime and object columns."""
    start_mem = df.memory_usage().sum() / 1024**2
    for col in df.columns:
        col_type = df[col].dtype
        
        # ── Skip datetime and object columns ──────────────────────
        if col_type == object or np.issubdtype(col_type, np.datetime64):
            continue
            
        c_min, c_max = df[col].min(), df[col].max()
        if str(col_type)[:3] == "int":
            for dtype in [np.int8, np.int16, np.int32, np.int64]:
                if c_min > np.iinfo(dtype).min and c_max < np.iinfo(dtype).max:
                    df[col] = df[col].astype(dtype)
                    break
        else:
            for dtype in [np.float16, np.float32, np.float64]:
                if c_min > np.finfo(dtype).min and c_max < np.finfo(dtype).max:
                    df[col] = df[col].astype(dtype)
                    break
    end_mem = df.memory_usage().sum() / 1024**2
    if verbose:
        print(f"  Memory: {start_mem:.2f} MB → {end_mem:.2f} MB  ({100*(start_mem-end_mem)/start_mem:.1f}% reduction)")
    return df

def smape(y_true, y_pred):
    """Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error — standard M5 metric."""
    y_true, y_pred = np.array(y_true), np.array(y_pred)
    denom = (np.abs(y_true) + np.abs(y_pred)) / 2
    mask  = denom > 0
    return np.mean(np.abs(y_true[mask] - y_pred[mask]) / denom[mask]) * 100

def mape(y_true, y_pred, eps=1e-6):
    """Mean Absolute Percentage Error."""
    y_true, y_pred = np.array(y_true), np.array(y_pred)
    return np.mean(np.abs((y_true - y_pred) / (y_true + eps))) * 100

def rmse(y_true, y_pred):
    return np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))

📊 Section 2: Data Loading¶

We load the three core M5 Forecasting Competition datasets:

File Description
sales_train_evaluation.csv Daily unit sales for 30,490 products × 1,941 days (wide format)
calendar.csv Date metadata — weekday, month, SNAP flags, special events
sell_prices.csv Weekly selling price per store–item combination

A random sample of SAMPLE_ITEMS items is selected for faster execution while preserving representativeness across all three M5 categories (Foods, Hobbies, Household).

# ── Stratified sampling across M5 categories ──────────────────────────────────
# Sample proportionally from Foods (>60%), Hobbies, Household to preserve category mix
np.random.seed(SEED)

category_counts = sales_raw["cat_id"].value_counts(normalize=True)
sample_per_cat  = (category_counts * SAMPLE_ITEMS).round().astype(int)
# Ensure we hit exactly SAMPLE_ITEMS
diff = SAMPLE_ITEMS - sample_per_cat.sum()
sample_per_cat.iloc[0] += diff   # adjust largest category

sampled_ids = []
for cat, n in sample_per_cat.items():
    ids = sales_raw[sales_raw["cat_id"] == cat]["id"].sample(n, random_state=SEED)
    sampled_ids.extend(ids.tolist())

sales = sales_raw[sales_raw["id"].isin(sampled_ids)].copy()
print(f"✅ Sampled {len(sales)} items  ({SAMPLE_ITEMS} requested)")
print(f"   Category breakdown: {sales['cat_id'].value_counts().to_dict()}")

🔍 Section 3: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Before modelling, we systematically explore the data to understand:

  • Data quality (missing values, zero sales)
  • Demand distribution by category and department
  • Temporal patterns (day-of-week seasonality, monthly trends, event spikes)
  • Price dynamics across stores

EDA findings will directly inform our feature engineering choices in Section 5.

🔄 Section 4: Data Preprocessing¶

Key steps:

  1. Wide → Long format: Unpivot daily columns into a single sales column
  2. Merge datasets: Attach calendar date info and selling prices
  3. Handle missing values: Fill missing prices with forward-fill (prices don't change mid-week)
  4. Type conversion: Ensure date is datetime64 and categoricals are encoded
In [37]:

# ── 4.4 Handle missing values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
print("🛠  Handling missing values...")

# Prices: forward-fill within each (store_id, item_id) group
df["sell_price"] = (
    df.sort_values("date")
      .groupby(["store_id","item_id"])["sell_price"]
      .transform(lambda x: x.fillna(method="ffill").fillna(method="bfill"))
)

# Event columns: fill NaN with "None"
for col in ["event_name_1","event_type_1","event_name_2","event_type_2"]:
    df[col] = df[col].fillna("None")

# SNAP columns: ensure int
for col in ["snap_CA","snap_TX","snap_WI"]:
    df[col] = df[col].fillna(0).astype(np.int8)

⚙️ Section 5: Feature Engineering¶

This is the most critical section for model performance. We engineer features that capture:

Feature Group Features Rationale
Lag features lag_1, lag_7, lag_14, lag_28 Yesterday, same-day last week/fortnight/month
Rolling stats rolling_7/14/28 mean & std Local trend and volatility
Price features sell_price, price_change Promotional and elasticity signal
Temporal dayofweek, month, year, weekofyear, quarter Seasonality at multiple scales
Calendar events is_event, is_snap, event encoding Demand spike on event days
Fourier terms sin/cos at weekly & yearly freq Smooth seasonality representation
In [42]:
# ── 5.1 Lag features ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
print("⚙️  Creating lag features...")

LAG_DAYS = [1, 7, 14, 28]

for lag in LAG_DAYS:
    df[f"lag_{lag}"] = (
        df.groupby("id")["sales"]
          .shift(lag)
    )
    print(f"  ✓ lag_{lag}")

print("✅ Lag features done.")

In [43]:
# ── 5.2 Rolling statistics ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
print("⚙️  Creating rolling statistics...")

ROLL_WINDOWS = [7, 14, 28]

for window in ROLL_WINDOWS:
    # Rolling mean on lag_1 (to prevent data leakage — we never see current day)
    df[f"rolling_mean_{window}"] = (
        df.groupby("id")["sales"]
          .transform(lambda x: x.shift(1).rolling(window, min_periods=1).mean())
    )
    df[f"rolling_std_{window}"]  = (
        df.groupby("id")["sales"]
          .transform(lambda x: x.shift(1).rolling(window, min_periods=1).std())
    )
    print(f"  ✓ rolling_mean_{window}, rolling_std_{window}")

# Expand mean (cumulative) — captures long-term average
df["expanding_mean"] = (
    df.groupby("id")["sales"]
      .transform(lambda x: x.shift(1).expanding().mean())
)
print("  ✓ expanding_mean")
print("✅ Rolling features done.")

# ── 5.4 Fourier seasonality features ─────────────────────────────────────────
print("⚙️  Creating Fourier terms for smooth seasonality...")

# Weekly cycle (period = 7 days)
df["sin_week"]  = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["dayofweek"] / 7)
df["cos_week"]  = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["dayofweek"] / 7)

# Yearly cycle (period = 365.25 days)
df["sin_year"]  = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["dayofyear"] / 365.25)
df["cos_year"]  = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["dayofyear"] / 365.25)

# Monthly cycle (2nd harmonic)
df["sin_month"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)
df["cos_month"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)

print("  ✓ sin/cos weekly, yearly, monthly Fourier terms")

# ── 5.5 Price-related features ────────────────────────────────────────────────
print("⚙️  Creating price features...")

# Fix: float16 breaks pandas diff/pct_change — upcast price to float32 first
df["sell_price"] = df["sell_price"].astype(np.float32)

# Price change week-over-week
df["price_change"] = (
    df.groupby("id")["sell_price"]
      .transform(lambda x: x.diff())
)
df["price_change_pct"] = (
    df.groupby("id")["sell_price"]
      .transform(lambda x: x.pct_change())
)

# Price relative to item's own mean (elasticity proxy)
df["price_vs_mean"] = (
    df.groupby("id")["sell_price"]
      .transform(lambda x: x / (x.mean() + 1e-6))
)

print("  ✓ price_change, price_change_pct, price_vs_mean")
print("✅ Price features done.")

🤖 Section 6: Model 1 — LightGBM (Primary Model)¶

LightGBM is the workhorse of demand forecasting competitions, including M5 itself.

Why LightGBM?

  • Handles tabular time-series features natively
  • Extremely fast on large datasets
  • Built-in feature importance with SHAP interpretability
  • Robust to missing values and mixed feature types

Training Strategy: Time-based split — last 28 days as test set (mimicking the M5 evaluation protocol).

In [52]:

# Use the last TEST_DAYS as hold-out — NEVER shuffle time series

train_df = df[df["date"] <= split_date].copy()
test_df  = df[df["date"]  > split_date].copy()

X_test  = test_df[FEATURE_COLS]

🔥 Section 7: Model 2 — LSTM (Deep Learning)¶

Long Short-Term Memory networks learn sequential demand patterns that tree-based models miss — such as gradual trend shifts and complex multi-lag dependencies.

Architecture:

  • Input: sequence of 28 time steps (1 month lookback)
  • 2 stacked LSTM layers with dropout
  • Fully-connected output layer → next 1-step prediction
  • Trained with Adam optimiser and MSE loss
In [56]:
# ── 7.1 Prepare LSTM dataset ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
# We train one shared LSTM on all sampled items for efficiency
# In production: one model per item cluster

SEQ_LEN     = 28      # look-back window
BATCH_SIZE  = 256
LSTM_EPOCHS = 30
LSTM_LR     = 1e-3

# Use only the numeric lag/rolling/temporal features (no string categoricals)
LSTM_FEATURES = [
    "lag_1","lag_7","lag_14","lag_28",
    "rolling_mean_7","rolling_mean_14","rolling_mean_28",
    "rolling_std_7","rolling_std_14",
    "sell_price","price_vs_mean",
    "dayofweek","month","is_weekend","is_event","is_snap_day",
    "sin_week","cos_week","sin_year","cos_year",
    "item_id_enc","store_id_enc","cat_id_enc"
]

class DemandSequenceDataset(Dataset):
    """
    Builds (X_sequence, y) pairs from a single time series.
    Each sample = SEQ_LEN consecutive feature vectors → next sales value.
    """
    def __init__(self, data_df, feature_cols, target_col, seq_len):
        # Normalise features (standard scaling per feature column)
        self.seq_len     = seq_len
        self.feature_cols = feature_cols
        self.target_col   = target_col
        
        feat_arr = data_df[feature_cols].values.astype(np.float32)
        tgt_arr  = data_df[target_col].values.astype(np.float32)
        
        # Per-feature normalisation
        self.feat_mean = feat_arr.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
        self.feat_std  = feat_arr.std(axis=0, keepdims=True) + 1e-6
        feat_norm      = (feat_arr - self.feat_mean) / self.feat_std
        
        # Target: log1p to stabilise variance
        self.tgt_mean = 0.0
        self.tgt_std  = 1.0
        tgt_norm      = np.log1p(tgt_arr)
        
        self.X = torch.tensor(feat_norm, dtype=torch.float32)
        self.y = torch.tensor(tgt_norm,  dtype=torch.float32)
    
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.X) - self.seq_len
    
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return (
            self.X[idx : idx + self.seq_len],       # (seq_len, n_features)
            self.y[idx + self.seq_len]               # scalar target
        )

# ── 7.2 Build LSTM model ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class LSTMDemandModel(nn.Module):
    """
    Stacked 2-layer LSTM encoder with fully-connected decoder.
    Architecture:
        Input (seq_len, n_features)
        → LSTM Layer 1 (hidden_dim, dropout)
        → LSTM Layer 2 (hidden_dim, dropout)
        → Last hidden state
        → FC Layer (hidden_dim → hidden_dim//2 → 1)
    """
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim=128, num_layers=2, dropout=0.2):
        super().__init__()
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(
            input_size  = input_dim,
            hidden_size = hidden_dim,
            num_layers  = num_layers,
            batch_first = True,
            dropout     = dropout if num_layers > 1 else 0.0
        )
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.fc = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim // 2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(dropout),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim // 2, 1)
        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (batch, seq_len, input_dim)
        lstm_out, (h_n, _) = self.lstm(x)
        # Use last hidden state of last layer
        last_hidden = h_n[-1]                     # (batch, hidden_dim)
        last_hidden = self.dropout(last_hidden)
        out = self.fc(last_hidden).squeeze(-1)    # (batch,)
        return out

n_lstm_features = len(LSTM_FEATURES)
lstm_model      = LSTMDemandModel(input_dim=n_lstm_features, hidden_dim=128, num_layers=2).to(DEVICE)

total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in lstm_model.parameters())
print(f"✅ LSTM model built | Parameters: {total_params:,}")
print(lstm_model)

  (dropout): Dropout(p=0.2, inplace=False)
  (fc): Sequential(
    (0): Linear(in_features=128, out_features=64, bias=True)
    (1): ReLU()
    (2): Dropout(p=0.2, inplace=False)
    (3): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=1, bias=True)
  )
)

# ── 7.3 Create datasets and dataloaders ──────────────────────────────────────
# Pick top-5 items by sales volume for LSTM (keep it tractable)
top_items = (
    train_df.groupby("id")["sales"].sum()
            .nlargest(5).index.tolist()
)

train_lstm_df = train_df[train_df["id"].isin(top_items)].copy()
test_lstm_df  = test_df[test_df["id"].isin(top_items)].copy()

train_dataset = DemandSequenceDataset(train_lstm_df, LSTM_FEATURES, TARGET, SEQ_LEN)
test_dataset  = DemandSequenceDataset(test_lstm_df,  LSTM_FEATURES, TARGET, SEQ_LEN)

train_loader  = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True,  drop_last=True)
test_loader   = DataLoader(test_dataset,  batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False, drop_last=False)

# ── 7.4 Training loop ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(lstm_model.parameters(), lr=LSTM_LR)
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(
    optimizer, patience=5, factor=0.5)

train_losses, val_losses = [], []

print(f"🚀 Training LSTM for {LSTM_EPOCHS} epochs on {DEVICE}...")
print(f"{'Epoch':>6} | {'Train Loss':>11} | {'Val Loss':>10} | {'LR':>8}")
print("-" * 45)

best_val_loss  = float("inf")
best_model_wts = None

for epoch in range(1, LSTM_EPOCHS + 1):
    # ── Training ────────────────────────────────
    lstm_model.train()
    running_loss = 0.0
    for X_batch, y_batch in train_loader:
        X_batch, y_batch = X_batch.to(DEVICE), y_batch.to(DEVICE)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        preds = lstm_model(X_batch)
        loss  = criterion(preds, y_batch)
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(lstm_model.parameters(), 1.0)   # gradient clipping
        optimizer.step()
        running_loss += loss.item() * len(X_batch)
    
    avg_train_loss = running_loss / len(train_dataset)
    
    # ── Validation ──────────────────────────────
    lstm_model.eval()
    val_loss = 0.0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for X_batch, y_batch in test_loader:
            X_batch, y_batch = X_batch.to(DEVICE), y_batch.to(DEVICE)
            preds = lstm_model(X_batch)
            val_loss += criterion(preds, y_batch).item() * len(X_batch)
    avg_val_loss = val_loss / max(len(test_dataset), 1)
    
    train_losses.append(avg_train_loss)
    val_losses.append(avg_val_loss)
    scheduler.step(avg_val_loss)
    
    if avg_val_loss < best_val_loss:
        best_val_loss  = avg_val_loss
        best_model_wts = {k: v.clone() for k, v in lstm_model.state_dict().items()}
    
    if epoch % 5 == 0 or epoch == 1:
        current_lr = optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"]
        print(f"{epoch:>6} | {avg_train_loss:>11.4f} | {avg_val_loss:>10.4f} | {current_lr:>8.6f}")

lstm_model.load_state_dict(best_model_wts)
print(f"\n✅ Best val loss: {best_val_loss:.4f}")

🚀 Section 8: Model 3 — Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)¶

The Temporal Fusion Transformer (Lim et al., 2019) is the state-of-the-art multi-horizon probabilistic forecasting model. Its key innovations:

  • Variable Selection Networks — automatically weight input features
  • LSTM encoder-decoder — captures local patterns
  • Multi-head attention — captures long-range temporal dependencies
  • Quantile outputs — produces P10/P50/P90 forecasts (uncertainty-aware)

📚 Paper: Temporal Fusion Transformers for Interpretable Multi-horizon Time Series Forecasting

In [65]:
# ── 8.1 Prepare TFT dataset ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
if not TFT_AVAILABLE:
    print("⚠️  pytorch-forecasting not available. Skipping TFT.")
else:
    MAX_ENCODER_LENGTH    = 28
    MAX_PREDICTION_LENGTH = 7

    tft_df = df.copy()
    tft_df = tft_df[tft_df["id"].isin(top_items)].copy()
    tft_df = tft_df.sort_values(["id","date"]).reset_index(drop=True)

    # Fix: TFT softplus normalizer requires float target — int8 from
    # reduce_mem_usage causes torch.finfo() to crash
    tft_df["sales"] = tft_df["sales"].astype(np.float32)

    # Also cast all known-future reals to float32 for safety
    float_cols = [
        "sell_price","dayofweek","month","is_weekend",
        "is_event","is_snap_day","sin_week","cos_week","sin_year","cos_year",
        "lag_1","rolling_mean_7"
    ]
    for col in float_cols:
        if col in tft_df.columns:
            tft_df[col] = tft_df[col].astype(np.float32)

    # Integer time index per item
    tft_df["time_idx"] = tft_df.groupby("id").cumcount()

    # Categoricals must be strings
    for col in ["id","cat_id","store_id","state_id"]:
        tft_df[col] = tft_df[col].astype(str)

    training_cutoff = tft_df["time_idx"].max() - MAX_PREDICTION_LENGTH

    print(f"✅ TFT dataframe ready | shape: {tft_df.shape}")
    print(f"   sales dtype      : {tft_df['sales'].dtype}")
    print(f"   Training cutoff  : {training_cutoff}")

# ── 8.3 Build and train TFT (memory-safe version) ────────────────────────────
if TFT_AVAILABLE:
    import gc
    gc.collect()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None

    # Use only 2 items and a shorter history to fit in RAM
    TFT_ITEMS            = top_items[:2]          # was 5 → use 2
    MAX_ENCODER_LENGTH   = 14                     # was 28 → 2 weeks
    MAX_PREDICTION_LENGTH = 3                     # was 7  → 3 days

    tft_df2 = tft_df[tft_df["id"].isin(TFT_ITEMS)].copy()
    training_cutoff2 = tft_df2["time_idx"].max() - MAX_PREDICTION_LENGTH

    training_dataset2 = TimeSeriesDataSet(
        tft_df2[tft_df2["time_idx"] <= training_cutoff2],
        time_idx               = "time_idx",
        target                 = "sales",
        group_ids              = ["id"],
        max_encoder_length     = MAX_ENCODER_LENGTH,
        max_prediction_length  = MAX_PREDICTION_LENGTH,
        time_varying_known_reals = [
            "time_idx", "sell_price",
            "dayofweek", "month", "is_weekend",
            "is_event", "sin_week", "cos_week",
        ],
        time_varying_unknown_reals = ["sales", "lag_1"],
        static_categoricals    = ["id", "cat_id"],
        target_normalizer      = GroupNormalizer(
            groups=["id"], transformation="softplus"
        ),
        add_relative_time_idx  = True,
        add_target_scales      = True,
        add_encoder_length     = True,
        allow_missing_timesteps= True,
    )

    validation_dataset2 = TimeSeriesDataSet.from_dataset(
        training_dataset2, tft_df2,
        predict=True, stop_randomization=True,
    )

    train_dataloader2 = training_dataset2.to_dataloader(
        train=True,  batch_size=16, num_workers=0, drop_last=True)
    val_dataloader2   = validation_dataset2.to_dataloader(
        train=False, batch_size=16, num_workers=0)

    # Smallest possible TFT architecture
    tft_model = TemporalFusionTransformer.from_dataset(
        training_dataset2,
        learning_rate           = 1e-3,
        hidden_size             = 8,      # was 32  → 8
        attention_head_size     = 1,      # was 2   → 1
        dropout                 = 0.1,
        hidden_continuous_size  = 4,      # was 16  → 4
        loss                    = QuantileLoss(),
        log_interval            = 5,
        reduce_on_plateau_patience = 2,
    )

    tft_params = sum(p.numel() for p in tft_model.parameters())
    print(f"✅ TFT model built | Parameters: {tft_params:,}")

    try:
        from lightning.pytorch import Trainer
    except ImportError:
        from pytorch_lightning import Trainer

    trainer = Trainer(
        max_epochs           = 10,        # was 15 → 10
        accelerator          = "cpu",     # force CPU — avoids CUDA OOM too
        gradient_clip_val    = 0.1,
        enable_model_summary = False,
        enable_progress_bar  = True,
        logger               = False,
    )

    print("\n🚀 Training TFT (lightweight mode)...")
    trainer.fit(
        tft_model,
        train_dataloaders = train_dataloader2,
        val_dataloaders   = val_dataloader2,
    )
    print("✅ TFT training complete.")

if TFT_AVAILABLE:
    try:
        # Predict using the TRAINING dataloader's validation split
        # (safer than val_dataloader2 which may have unseen category indices)
        tft_raw_predictions = tft_model.predict(
            val_dataloader2,
            return_y     = True,
            return_index = True,
            mode         = "raw",           # returns full output dict
        )

        # Extract P10 / P50 / P90 from quantile output
        # Shape: (n_samples, prediction_length, n_quantiles)
        pred_tensor      = tft_raw_predictions.output["prediction"]
        tft_preds_p50    = pred_tensor[:, :, 3].detach().numpy()   # median (q=0.5)
        tft_preds_p10    = pred_tensor[:, :, 0].detach().numpy()
        tft_preds_p90    = pred_tensor[:, :, 6].detach().numpy()
        tft_actuals      = tft_raw_predictions.y[0].numpy()

        tft_preds_flat   = tft_preds_p50.flatten().clip(0)
        tft_actuals_flat = tft_actuals.flatten().clip(0)

        print("── TFT Test Metrics (P50) ───────────────────────────────")
        print(f"  MAE   : {mean_absolute_error(tft_actuals_flat, tft_preds_flat):.4f}")
        print(f"  RMSE  : {rmse(tft_actuals_flat, tft_preds_flat):.4f}")
        print(f"  MAPE  : {mape(tft_actuals_flat, tft_preds_flat):.2f}%")

🧠 Section 9: Ensemble Model — Weighted Average¶

Combining predictions from multiple models reduces variance and improves generalisation — a well-established principle in competition forecasting.

Strategy: Inverse-MAE weighted average

  • Models with lower MAE receive proportionally higher weight
  • Simple, interpretable, and surprisingly competitive
In [72]:
# ── 9.1 Align predictions to common index ─────────────────────────────────────
# LightGBM predicts on full test set; LSTM and TFT on top-5 items only
# We use LightGBM as the base for ensemble (full coverage) and boost it with LSTM

# For items in top_items: use weighted ensemble
# For remaining items: use LightGBM only

print("🔀 Building ensemble predictions...")

# Compute individual MAEs on available predictions
lgb_mae_val  = mean_absolute_error(y_test, lgb_preds)
lstm_mae_val = mean_absolute_error(lstm_targets_raw, lstm_preds_raw)
tft_mae_val  = mean_absolute_error(tft_actuals_flat, tft_preds_flat)

print(f"  LightGBM MAE : {lgb_mae_val:.4f}")
print(f"  LSTM MAE     : {lstm_mae_val:.4f}")
print(f"  TFT MAE      : {tft_mae_val:.4f}")

# Inverse-MAE weights
inv_mae = np.array([1/lgb_mae_val, 1/lstm_mae_val, 1/tft_mae_val])
weights  = inv_mae / inv_mae.sum()

print(f"\n  Ensemble Weights:")
print(f"    LightGBM : {weights[0]:.3f}")
print(f"    LSTM     : {weights[1]:.3f}")
print(f"    TFT      : {weights[2]:.3f}")

# ── 9.2 Ensemble on top items (all 3 models available) ───────────────────────
# Align LSTM preds to test_df for top items
top_test_df = test_df[test_df["id"].isin(top_items)].copy()

# LSTM predictions are ordered per item — map them
lstm_pred_map = {}
lstm_idx = 0
for item in top_items:
    item_df = test_lstm_df[test_lstm_df["id"] == item]
    n = max(len(item_df) - SEQ_LEN, 0)
    lstm_pred_map[item] = lstm_preds_raw[lstm_idx: lstm_idx + n]
    lstm_idx += n

# TFT predictions (already on top items, max_pred_length steps)
tft_available_flag = TFT_AVAILABLE and len(tft_preds_flat) > 0

# Full ensemble predictions for all test rows
ensemble_preds = lgb_preds.copy()   # default = LightGBM

# For top items where LSTM gives coverage, blend
for item in top_items:
    mask      = test_df["id"] == item
    mask_idx  = np.where(mask)[0]
    n_lstm    = len(lstm_pred_map.get(item, []))
    if n_lstm > 0:
        # Overlap region
        overlap_idx = mask_idx[:n_lstm]
        lgb_overlap  = lgb_preds[overlap_idx]
        lstm_overlap = lstm_pred_map[item][:len(overlap_idx)]
        
        # 2-model blend (TFT weights absorbed if unavailable)
        w_lgb  = weights[0] / (weights[0] + weights[1])
        w_lstm = weights[1] / (weights[0] + weights[1])
        ensemble_preds[overlap_idx] = (
            w_lgb * lgb_overlap + w_lstm * lstm_overlap
        ).clip(0)

ensemble_mae  = mean_absolute_error(y_test, ensemble_preds)
ensemble_rmse = rmse(y_test, ensemble_preds)
ensemble_mape = mape(y_test.values, ensemble_preds)

print("── Ensemble Test Metrics ────────────────────────────────")
print(f"  MAE   : {ensemble_mae:.4f}  (vs LightGBM: {lgb_mae_val:.4f})")
print(f"  RMSE  : {ensemble_rmse:.4f}")
print(f"  MAPE  : {ensemble_mape:.2f}%")
print(f"\n📌 Ensemble {'improved' if ensemble_mae < lgb_mae_val else 'matched'} over LightGBM baseline.")

⚠️ Section 10: Anomaly Detection — Isolation Forest¶

In quick-commerce, demand anomalies (sudden spikes or drops) can represent:

  • 🏏 IPL match nights → snack/beverage spike
  • 🌧️ Rain events → hot food demand spike
  • 🚨 Supply shocks → sudden zero demand
  • 📱 Flash sales or app promotions → abnormal uplift

We use Isolation Forest — an ensemble of random trees that isolates anomalies by the number of splits required. Anomalies require fewer splits because they're extreme values far from the distribution centre.

In [74]:
# ── 10.1 Build anomaly feature matrix ─────────────────────────────────────────
print("⚠️  Running Isolation Forest anomaly detection...")

# Features for anomaly detection: residuals + context features
test_df_anom = test_df.copy()
test_df_anom["residual"]      = np.abs(y_test.values - ensemble_preds)
test_df_anom["pct_error"]     = test_df_anom["residual"] / (y_test.values + 1e-6)

anom_features = [
    "residual","pct_error",
    "lag_1","lag_7",
    "rolling_mean_7","rolling_std_7",
    "sell_price","is_event","is_snap_day",
    "dayofweek","month"
]

X_anom = test_df_anom[anom_features].fillna(0)

# ── 10.2 Train Isolation Forest ───────────────────────────────────────────────
iso_forest = IsolationForest(
    n_estimators = 200,
    contamination= 0.05,     # expect ~5% anomalies (demand spike days)
    random_state = SEED,
    n_jobs       = -1
)

iso_forest.fit(X_anom)
anomaly_scores  = iso_forest.decision_function(X_anom)    # more negative = more anomalous
anomaly_labels  = iso_forest.predict(X_anom)              # -1 = anomaly, 1 = normal

test_df_anom["anomaly_score"] = anomaly_scores
test_df_anom["is_anomaly"]    = (anomaly_labels == -1).astype(int)

n_anomalies = test_df_anom["is_anomaly"].sum()
print(f"✅ Anomalies detected : {n_anomalies} / {len(test_df_anom)} rows ({n_anomalies/len(test_df_anom)*100:.1f}%)")

📈 Section 11: Model Evaluation — Comprehensive Metrics¶

We compare all models on four metrics:

Metric Formula Interpretation
MAE mean( y - ŷ ) Average absolute error in same units as sales
RMSE √mean((y-ŷ)²) Penalises large errors — important for spike events
MAPE mean( y-ŷ /y) × 100 Relative % error — scale-independent
SMAPE mean( y-ŷ /(( y + ŷ )/2)) × 100 Symmetric MAPE — M5 competition standard
In [77]:
# ── 11.1 Compute metrics for all models ───────────────────────────────────────
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

def eval_metrics(name, y_true, y_pred):
    y_true = np.array(y_true).flatten()
    y_pred = np.array(y_pred).flatten()
    min_len = min(len(y_true), len(y_pred))
    y_true, y_pred = y_true[:min_len], y_pred[:min_len]
    return {
        "Model" : name,
        "MAE"   : round(mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "RMSE"  : round(rmse(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "MAPE"  : round(mape(y_true, y_pred), 2),
        "SMAPE" : round(smape(y_true, y_pred), 2),
    }

results = [
    eval_metrics("LightGBM",          y_test.values,        lgb_preds),
    eval_metrics("LSTM",              lstm_targets_raw,      lstm_preds_raw),
    eval_metrics("TFT (P50)",         tft_actuals_flat,      tft_preds_flat),
    eval_metrics("Ensemble",          y_test.values,         ensemble_preds),
]

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).set_index("Model")

print("═" * 58)
print("         Q-Cast Model Evaluation Results")
print("═" * 58)
print(results_df.to_string())
print("═" * 58)
print(f"\n✅ Best MAE   : {results_df['MAE'].idxmin()} ({results_df['MAE'].min():.4f})")
print(f"✅ Best RMSE  : {results_df['RMSE'].idxmin()} ({results_df['RMSE'].min():.4f})")
print(f"✅ Best SMAPE : {results_df['SMAPE'].idxmin()} ({results_df['SMAPE'].min():.2f}%)")

💡 Bonus: Business Impact Simulation — Q-Cast vs Baseline¶

We simulate a simple inventory policy over the test period to measure the business value of better forecasting.

Policy:

  • Each day, we stock forecast × (1 + safety_factor) units
  • If actual demand > stock → stockout (lost sales)
  • If actual demand < stock AND items are perishable → waste

We compare three strategies:

  1. Naive: Reorder = last day's sales (baseline)
  2. Moving Average: 7-day rolling mean
  3. Q-Cast Ensemble: Our model's forecast
In [82]:
# ── Business simulation ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SAFETY_FACTOR = 0.10     # 10% safety buffer

def simulate_inventory(y_true, y_pred, safety=SAFETY_FACTOR):
    """
    Simulate daily inventory decisions.
    Returns stockout_rate, waste_rate, fill_rate.
    """
    y_true = np.array(y_true)
    y_pred = np.array(y_pred).clip(0)
    
    stocked       = (y_pred * (1 + safety)).round()
    stockout_units= np.maximum(y_true - stocked, 0)
    waste_units   = np.maximum(stocked - y_true, 0)
    
    stockout_rate = stockout_units.sum() / y_true.sum() * 100
    waste_rate    = waste_units.sum()    / stocked.sum() * 100
    fill_rate     = 100 - stockout_rate
    
    return stockout_rate, waste_rate, fill_rate

# ── Naive baseline: yesterday's sales
naive_preds   = test_df["lag_1"].values.clip(0)

# ── Moving average baseline: 7-day rolling mean
ma_preds      = test_df["rolling_mean_7"].values.clip(0)

# ── Simulate all strategies
s_naive   = simulate_inventory(y_test, naive_preds)
s_ma      = simulate_inventory(y_test, ma_preds)
s_qcast   = simulate_inventory(y_test, ensemble_preds)

# ── Summary table
biz_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Strategy"      : ["Naive (Yesterday)","Moving Average (7d)","Q-Cast Ensemble"],
    "Stockout Rate %" : [s_naive[0], s_ma[0], s_qcast[0]],
    "Waste Rate %"  : [s_naive[1], s_ma[1], s_qcast[1]],
    "Fill Rate %"   : [s_naive[2], s_ma[2], s_qcast[2]],
})
biz_results = biz_results.round(2)

print("═" * 60)
print("         Q-Cast Business Impact Simulation")
print("═" * 60)
print(biz_results.to_string(index=False))
print("═" * 60)

stockout_imp = (s_ma[0] - s_qcast[0]) / s_ma[0] * 100
waste_imp    = (s_ma[1] - s_qcast[1]) / s_ma[1] * 100
print(f"\n📌 Q-Cast vs Moving Average baseline:")
print(f"   Stockout reduction : {stockout_imp:+.1f}%")
print(f"   Waste reduction    : {waste_imp:+.1f}%")

📋 Section 13: Final Summary & Next Steps¶

Model Performance Summary¶

Model Key Strength Best Use Case
LightGBM Fast, interpretable, handles sparse data Production workhorse — all items
LSTM Captures sequential temporal dependencies High-velocity SKUs with smooth demand
TFT Multi-horizon, uncertainty quantification Strategic planning, 7-14 day horizon
Ensemble Best of all worlds, reduced variance Final production forecasts

Q-Cast Value Proposition¶

  • ✅ Demonstrated demand forecasting with MAE/RMSE/SMAPE evaluation
  • ✅ 3-model pipeline (LightGBM + LSTM + TFT) with ensemble combination
  • ✅ Automated anomaly detection (Isolation Forest, 3 alert types)
  • ✅ Business simulation showing quantified stockout and waste reduction
  • ✅ MSc-level feature engineering (lags, rolling stats, Fourier, price, events)

Next Steps for Production¶

  1. Scale to all 30,490 M5 items using parallelised training
  2. Integrate real-time synthetic simulator (FastAPI + Redis queue)
  3. Deploy MinT hierarchical reconciliation for coherent multi-level forecasts
  4. Connect Streamlit dashboard for live monitoring
  5. MLflow experiment tracking for model versioning
  6. Docker Compose for one-command deployment
